title: India's New-Age Space Technologies
subtitle: The Road to Self-Reliance
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                28 OCT 2026 12:19PM by PIB Delhi
content:
India’s space journey began in 1963 with a sounding rocket launched from Thumba, Kerala. It now looks ahead to the planned Bharatiya Antariksh Station. New technologies are driving this progress. They include reusable launch vehicles, electric, green and nuclear propulsion, and in-orbit servicing. Through SpaDeX, India also became the fourth country to achieve autonomous docking of two spacecraft in orbit. These advances strengthen self-reliance. Meanwhile, Gaganyaan is advancing India’s human spaceflight goals.
Space Science & Relevance for Today
India’s organised space activities began in 1962 with the establishment of the Indian National Committee for Space Research (INCOSPAR) under the vision of Dr Vikram A. Sarabhai. The first sounding rocket was launched from Thumba, Kerala on 21 November 1963. The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) was formed on 15 August 1969, superseding INCOSPAR, and was subsequently brought under the Department of Space in 1972. Since its inception, ISRO followed a development-first philosophy: using space technology to solve problems on the ground. Over the decades, it grew far beyond a launch service provider, and its efficiency and technical excellence have earned global recognition. That reputation now rests on a simple promise: every mission must serve the common citizen.
That vision now shapes daily life across the country.
Communication satellites
extend connectivity to remote and underserved areas.
Earth observation data
support agriculture, disaster assessment, planning, environmental monitoring and other national requirements.
Weather satellites
track cyclones and monsoons, enabling early warnings that save lives. Fishermen, farmers and coastal communities rely on these alerts to protect their livelihoods. These systems connect citizens, protect communities, strengthen governance and drive inclusive, sustainable growth. Beyond these services, space also guards India’s frontiers and shapes its future.
Space-based communication
systems support national security and strategic requirements.
Building on these strengths, emerging technologies are opening fresh avenues for innovation, connectivity and service delivery. Private enterprises and start-ups are now joining this journey. This positions India as a confident, self-reliant and globally respected space power.
Click To Read More in Detail: India's Space Odyssey
Creative Minds, Catalyzing Science, Empowering Technologies
ESTIC-2026, the second edition of India's Emerging Science, Technology and Innovation Conclave. ESTIC 2026 is being scheduled for 27–29 October 2026 at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi. The Space Science & Technologies thematic session, organised by the Department of Space/ISRO on 29 October 2026, is one of the conclave’s thematic programmes.
Read More on Agenda:
ESTIC 2026
Emerging Space Technologies
As India moves toward greater self-reliance and bolder goals, a new generation of technologies is taking shape to power this journey. These innovations span
next-generation launch systems, in-space operations, human spaceflight, and advanced navigation and communications
. They mark a shift from India’s early achievements to a future-ready space programme. Built for the decades ahead, these associated programmes aim to keep India competitive, connected and firmly self-reliant.
Next-Generation Launch Vehicles (NGLV)
Access to space begins with the ability to launch. A country that can build and fly its own rockets decides when, how and at what cost it reaches space. India’s launch journey has moved from small, single-use (expendable) rockets to heavy-lift vehicles, and it is now moving towards reusable systems.
India's Traditional Launch Vehicles
PSLV (Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle
):
PSLV (Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle), ISRO’s workhorse, can carry up to 1,750 kg to a 600-km Sun-Synchronous Polar Orbit (SSPO) and up to 1,425 kg to Sub-Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit (Sub-GTO), depending on mission configuration.
GSLV (Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle):
It uses the indigenous Cryogenic Upper Stage and can carry communication satellites of up to the 2-tonne class.
LVM3 (Launch Vehicle Mark-3)
is India’s heavy-lift launch vehicle. It can carry communication satellites of the 4-tonne class to Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit (GTO), and payloads of the 10-tonne class to Low Earth Orbit (LEO).
SSLV (Small Satellite Launch Vehicle):
SSLV is a three-stage vehicle weighing ~120 tonnes at lift-off. It can launch satellites of up to the ~500-kg class into a 500-km planar orbit.
In September 2024, the Union Cabinet approved the development of the
Next Generation Launch Vehicle (NGLV).
The approved
outlay of ₹
8,240
crore covers development costs, three developmental flights, essential facilities, programme management and the launch campaign. Designed for a maximum capacity of
30 tonnes to Low Earth Orbit (LEO)
, the
NGLV
triples India's current launch payload capability compared to the
10-tonne LEO limit
of the LVM3. In addition, a partially reusable NGLV variant with a 14-tonne LEO payload capability is being developed to support lower-cost access to space. Its
reusability feature
will also lower the cost of reaching space.
NGLV will enable both national and commercial missions. These include human spaceflight missions to the
Bharatiya Antariksh Station
, as well as
lunar
and
interplanetary exploration
. It will also launch communication and earth observation satellite constellations to Low Earth Orbit. These missions will benefit the entire space ecosystem and boost the nation’s capability and capacity.
Understanding Key Terms
Sun-Synchronous Orbit (SSO):
A Sun-Synchronous Orbit (SSO) is a near-polar orbit in which a satellite passes over an area at approximately the same local solar time, enabling comparisons under similar illumination. The interval between repeat observations of a particular location varies with the satellite and its orbit.
Geostationary Transfer Orbit (GTO):
GTO is an elliptical intermediate orbit used to transfer a satellite into geostationary orbit (GEO). Its lowest point (perigee) is typically a few hundred kilometres above Earth, while its highest point (apogee) is near 35,786 km above Earth's surface. The launch vehicle typically places the satellite in GTO rather than directly into GEO. Near apogee, the satellite fires its onboard apogee motor to raise its perigee and circularise the orbit. Additional manoeuvres may be required to align the orbit with Earth's equatorial plane. In GEO, the satellite orbits above the equator with a period matching Earth's rotation, appearing stationary relative to the ground.
Cryogenic Upper Stage
:
A cryogenic upper stage is the final stage of a launch vehicle that uses these propellants to provide the high efficiency needed to place satellites into their intended orbits. ISRO’s indigenous cryogenic upper stage used on GSLV employs liquid hydrogen (LH₂) as fuel and liquid oxygen (LOX) as oxidiser, both stored at extremely low temperatures. It replaced the Russian-supplied stage used in earlier GSLV flights, strengthening India’s self-reliance in advanced launch vehicle technology.
Reusable Launch Vehicle (RLV)
RLV technologies
can help reduce launch costs and improve operational efficiency. Unlike conventional expendable (single-use) launch vehicles, reusable systems are designed to recover major components for subsequent missions. Their development requires controlled atmospheric re-entry, autonomous navigation, aerodynamic flight and precision landing. ISRO has demonstrated autonomous runway-landing technologies using its winged Reusable Launch Vehicle technology demonstrator, Pushpak. The three RLV Landing Experiments were completed on 2 April 2023, 22 March 2024 and 23 June 2024, respectively. LEX-03 validated autonomous landing under more challenging cross-range and wind conditions.
Scramjet Technology: Powering India’s Reusable Space Transportation
A scramjet (supersonic combustion ramjet) is an air-breathing jet engine. It carries only fuel and draws oxygen from the surrounding air. Conventional rockets haul both fuel and oxidiser. A scramjet is therefore lighter and can deliver more payload for the same lift-off mass. It works only within the atmosphere at very high velocity, so a booster must first accelerate it. Its velocity is expressed as a Mach number. Mach 1 equals the speed of sound. Anything above Mach 5 is called hypersonic. Scramjets can complement reusable launch vehicles, which retrieve and refly major parts to cut costs. They offer a promising path to affordable space access.
India flight-tested its
scramjet in 28 August 2016
. It reached Mach 6, a hypersonic velocity, making the country the fourth to demonstrate this.
On 22 July 2024, ISRO separately conducted an experimental
RH-560
sounding-rocket flight
to demonstrate air-breathing propulsion systems and assess their performance.
Indigenous Space Hardware and Critical Technologies
Every space mission relies on critical technologies, including engines, thrusters, fuels and power systems. Developing these technologies within India helps reduce dependence on foreign suppliers and strengthens the country’s ability to build and operate spacecraft independently. ISRO is advancing indigenous propulsion technologies, including electric propulsion and alternative fuels. It is also exploring technologies for future missions. These efforts contribute to India’s long-term goal of self-reliance in space.
One important area of progress is
electric propulsion
, which uses electrical energy to accelerate propellant and generate thrust. Compared with conventional chemical propulsion, it can achieve the same orbital changes using much less propellant. This reduces the fuel carried by a satellite and frees up mass for communication equipment and other payloads. On 27 March 2025, ISRO successfully completed a 1,000-hour life test of its
indigenous 300 mN stationary plasma thruster
. Its
specific impulse
, a measure of propulsion efficiency, is at least six times that of conventional propulsion systems. ISRO plans to validate the technology aboard its Technology Demonstration Satellite (TDS-01). It is intended to support future electric-propulsion satellites, including orbit raising and station keeping.
Alongside electric propulsion, ISRO is developing alternative propellants to reduce environmental impacts and improve propulsion efficiency i.e.,
Green Propulsion.
One example is
ISROSENE
, a rocket-grade kerosene. Liquid oxygen–kerosene propellants are being developed for semicryogenic rocket-engine applications.
Progress in green propulsion also extends beyond ISRO’s own development programmes. Under DRDO’s
Technology Development Fund
, Bengaluru-based Bellatrix Aerospace developed a 1 N-class green monopropellant thruster for microsatellite attitude control and orbit keeping. Its in-orbit functionality was demonstrated on a payload launched aboard PSLV-C58 in January 2024.
These developments illustrate India’s progress in indigenous electric and green propulsion technologies. Continued testing and validation will help determine their readiness for wider use in future space missions.
Radioisotope Heating and Power Technologies
ISRO and
Department of Atomic Energy (DAE)
are collaborating on requirements for
Radioisotope Heater Units (RHU)
, which supply heat, and
Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generators (RTG)
, which convert radioisotope heat into electrical power ISRO is collaborating with the DAE on RHU and RTG requirements for possible future Chandrayaan and Mars missions.
In-Space Operations and Human Spaceflight
In-space operations are the activities spacecraft carry out once they are in orbit, such as
rendezvous, docking and undocking.
Launching a satellite is only the first step: complex missions such as a space station, a crewed flight or a lunar sample return depend on what spacecraft can do after launch. In-space docking technology is essential when multiple rocket launches are needed to achieve common mission objectives, and it underpins ambitions such as sample return from the Moon and the building and operation of the Bharatiya Antariksh Station.
ISRO’s SpaDeX mission first docked its two satellites on 16 January 2025 and subsequently demonstrated undocking. A second docking was completed with full autonomy from an inter-satellite distance of 15 m on 20th April 2025. Bidirectional power transfer between the docked satellites was demonstrated on 21st April 2025.
India thereby became the fourth country to demonstrate space docking, after the United States, Russia and China
. This achievement also advances technologies required for future missions.
Beyond joining spacecraft, docking enables them to work together in orbit. In-orbit servicing could, in future, enable refuelling, repair or upgrading of spacecraft in orbit, without bringing them back to Earth. SpaDeX demonstrated docking, undocking and power transfer. These interventions can extend satellite lifespans and reduce the need for replacement missions. These achievements provide important technological building blocks for developing future in-orbit servicing capabilities.
Next-Generation Navigation and Communications
Satellite navigation and communication systems support essential services across India. Navigation satellites provide positioning, navigation and timing information, while communication satellites relay television, telephone, broadband and other data signals. Together, these systems support transportation, financial services, telecommunications, disaster management and national security. India is strengthening these capabilities through ISRO’s indigenous NavIC navigation system and communication satellites.
Navigation with Indian Constellation (NavIC)
is India’s independent regional satellite
navigation system
, developed and maintained by ISRO. It provides positioning, navigation and timing services across India and up to 1,500 kilometres beyond the Indian mainland. NavIC offers a
Standard Positioning Service
for civilian users and
an encrypted Restricted Service for authorized users
. These capabilities support terrestrial, aerial and maritime navigation, surveying, vehicle tracking and precise timing. NavIC also supports
emergency warning messages
for fishermen operating beyond terrestrial network coverage. Its integration into compatible devices and applications can further expand its use across civilian and strategic sectors.
Additionally, India’s
communication satellites
support broadcasting, broadband connectivity and secure communications. GSAT-24, launched aboard Ariane-5 from Kourou, French Guiana, on 23 June 2022 at 03:20 IST (22 June local time), was realised to meet Direct-to-Home (DTH) television requirements in India. Building on this capability, GSAT-N2 (GSAT-20) was launched on 19 November 2024. This high-throughput satellite has a capacity of approximately 48 Gbps and is designed to support broadband and in-flight connectivity across India, including remote island regions.
Communication satellites also serve
India’s defence requirements
. CMS-03, also known as GSAT-7R, was launched on 2 November 2025. It is a dedicated communication satellite for the Indian Navy. These satellites strengthen India's space-based communication infrastructure and support civilian connectivity, maritime operations and national security.
Advanced Earth Observation Satellites
Earth observation satellites monitor the land, oceans, ice-covered regions and atmosphere from space. Their data supports agriculture, disaster management, water resource planning, climate research and national security. Between December 2020 and December 2025, ISRO launched 22 satellites, including seven Earth observation satellites. These satellites provide images and data for monitoring natural resources, tracking environmental changes and supporting informed planning. India continues to strengthen these capabilities through advanced technologies, including radar imaging and hyperspectral observation.
A major advancement in Earth observation is the
NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR) mission
. It was launched on 30 July 2025 aboard GSLV-F16 from Sriharikota. It is the first satellite mission to use two radar frequencies together: NASA’s L-band and ISRO’s S-band. Radar can collect data through clouds and in darkness, enabling observations in almost all-weather conditions, both day and night. NISAR is designed to observe the Earth’s land and ice-covered surfaces every 12 days. Its data can help scientists monitor ground deformation, glacier movement, vegetation changes, soil moisture and natural hazards. These observations can also support coastal monitoring and disaster response.
While radar reveals changes in the Earth’s surface, hyperspectral imaging helps identify different materials and surface characteristics. ISRO launched the
Hyperspectral Imaging Satellite (HysIS)
on 29 November 2018. It observes the Earth’s surface in visible, near-infrared and shortwave-infrared wavelengths. By recording information across numerous narrow bands of light, HysIS can distinguish features that ordinary imaging may not readily identify. Its data supports applications in agriculture, forestry, soil and geological studies, coastal zones and inland waters.
Did You Know?
HysIS was launched alongside 30 foreign satellites from eight countries. These comprised one micro-satellite and 29 nano-satellites. The participating countries were Australia, Canada, Colombia, Finland, Malaysia, the Netherlands, Spain and the United States. Of these, 23 satellites were from the United States. The launch also demonstrated PSLV’s capability to deploy multiple satellites for international customers.
Way Forward: Building a US$44 Billion Space Economy
India’s space sector is increasingly contributing to economic growth, private investment and industrial capability, alongside its scientific and strategic goals. As per the Department of Space, India’s space economy is targeted to reach US$44 billion by 2033. Emerging technologies such as reusable launch vehicles, air-breathing propulsion, electric propulsion and in-space docking are supporting this growth.
This technological momentum is already creating economic opportunity. NewSpace India Limited (NSIL) has signed 118 Technology Transfer Agreements to transfer 83 technologies developed by ISRO to Indian industry. As a result, investor confidence is also growing. Cumulative investment in Indian space start-ups reached approximately US$618.5 million as of 31 March 2026, with funding shifting from early-stage seed support to larger, growth-stage rounds.
Together, these developments show that India's emerging space technologies are not only advancing national capability but also building a strong, enterprise-led space economy for the years ahead.

title: Green Hydrogen
subtitle: Emerging Pillar of India’s Clean Energy Transition
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                28 OCT 2026 11:15AM by PIB Delhi
content:
Green hydrogen is emerging as a pillar of India’s clean energy transition. It is produced by splitting water using renewable electricity. It can help reduce emissions in sectors such as fertiliser production, petroleum refining, iron and steel manufacturing, heavy-duty road transport and shipping
.
The National Green Hydrogen Mission (NGHM) supports domestic manufacturing, production, assured demand and credible certification. From green ammonia auctions to India’s first hydrogen train, early projects point to a promising path.
Why Green Hydrogen
Hydrogen is an energy carrier that stores energy and delivers it for varied uses. In a fuel cell, it reacts with oxygen to produce electricity, leaving only water and heat as by-products, and no polluting compounds or greenhouse gases. Although pure hydrogen is not found in large quantities in nature,  it can be extracted from compounds such as water or natural gas. Its environmental impact therefore depends on how it is made. Conventional methods rely on fossil fuels and release carbon emissions.
Production using renewable electricity from solar and wind power can cut this footprint substantially. Hydrogen made by splitting water using renewable power is called
green hydrogen
. Unlike fossil-based routes, this process emits far less carbon. India’s abundant solar and wind resources make domestic production feasible. This diversifies the country’s energy sources and strengthens energy security. It also supports India’s goal of net-zero emissions by 2070.
Green hydrogen matters most in sectors where cutting emissions is difficult. Reasons include high-temperature heat needs, chemical processes and few alternatives to fossil fuels.
These hard-to-abate sectors
include fertiliser, petroleum refining, iron and steel, heavy-duty road transport and shipping. Fertiliser and refining plants already use hydrogen, so green hydrogen can replace the fossil-based supply. It can also support lower-emission steelmaking, selected transport uses and energy storage. It is especially useful where direct electrification is difficult or less practical.
For India, wider adoption could reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels. It would also lessen exposure to global fuel price swings. The sector could open opportunities in manufacturing, draw investment, create jobs and expand exports. Building capabilities across the value chain would strengthen domestic supply chains and spur industrial innovation. Green hydrogen can thus support self-reliance, sustainable industrial growth and a low-carbon future.
What Makes Hydrogen “Green”
Hydrogen releases no carbon dioxide when used, so its climate impact depends on how it is produced. In August 2023, the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE) notified India’s Green Hydrogen Standard. Hydrogen qualifies as green if emissions do not exceed 2 kg of CO₂ equivalent per kg of hydrogen, on a well-to-gate basis, measured as a 12-month average. India thus became one of the first few countries to define green hydrogen formally.
Creative Minds, Catalyzing Science, Empowering Technologies
ESTIC-2026, the second edition of India’s Emerging Science, Technology and Innovation Conclave, is being held from 27–29 October 2026 at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi. Organised by the Council of Scientific & Industrial Research (CSIR), the conclave follows the theme “Creative Minds, Catalyzing Science, Empowering Technologies.” It advances emerging frontiers in science and technology, including energy technologies such as
Green Hydrogen Technology.
Spanning 12 thematic areas, ESTIC-2026 features plenary sessions, technical discussions and exhibitions. The conclave also promotes strategic collaborations in support of India’s vision of Viksit Bharat 2047.

ESTIC 2026
How Is Green Hydrogen Produced?
Green hydrogen is produced mainly through water (H₂O) electrolysis. Electrolysis uses electricity to split a compound into simpler substances. Here, renewable electricity splits water into hydrogen (H₂) and oxygen (O₂), with minimal emissions.
2H2O
→
2H2   +   O2
The key equipment is the
electrolyser.
It contains
two electrodes
, a cathode and an anode, connected to a power source. They operate within an
electrolyte,
which helps ions move through the cell. A
diaphragm
keeps the gases apart while allowing ions to pass. When
current flows
, hydrogen forms at the cathode and oxygen at the anode. The gases are collected separately for further usage. An electrolyser thus turns renewable electricity and water into a low-emission fuel for industry, transport and other uses.
Did You Know?
Water is purified before electrolysis, because impurities can damage cells and shorten their life. According to MNRE, about nine litres of demineralised water is needed per kg of hydrogen. Afterwards, the hydrogen is dried and purified before compression. India’s Green Hydrogen Standard counts emissions from each of these steps.
Applications of Green Hydrogen
Fertilisers:
Ammonia, made from hydrogen and nitrogen, is the base for nitrogen fertilisers such as urea. Most of this hydrogen now comes from natural gas. Green hydrogen can replace it and yield green ammonia with far lower emissions.
Petroleum refineries:
Refineries use hydrogen to remove sulphur from petrol and diesel, so the fuels burn cleaner. They also use it to upgrade heavy oil into lighter fuels such as diesel, aviation turbine fuel and naphtha. These fuels serve road transport, aviation and industry. Most refinery hydrogen comes from fossil fuels, so a green supply can cut refining emissions.
Steel:
Conventional steelmaking uses coal to strip oxygen from iron ore, releasing carbon dioxide. In direct reduced iron routes, green hydrogen can do this job instead. The reduction stage then releases water vapour in place of carbon dioxide.
City gas networks:
Green hydrogen can be blended with natural gas in limited proportions, subject to safety standards and infrastructure compatibility. This allows existing gas networks to supply a hydrogen-natural gas blend to homes, businesses and industries. Such blending can reduce fossil fuel consumption and associated emissions while utilising existing distribution infrastructure.
Road and rail transport:
Fuel-cell vehicles convert hydrogen into electricity on board, which drives electric motors. Their only emission at the point of use is water vapour. This suits buses, trucks and trains that need long range and quick refuelling.
Did You Know?
India’s first indigenous hydrogen-powered train was inaugurated on 17 July 2026 on the Jind–Sonipat section. The 10-car trainset can carry around 2,600 passengers. A facility at Jind stores nearly 3,000 kg of hydrogen. The train emits only water vapour and heat. Click to
Read More
Shipping:
Green hydrogen can be converted into green ammonia and green methanol, which can fuel ships. These can replace conventional marine fuels on long voyages. Adoption depends on engine compatibility, safety requirements and port infrastructure.
Exports:
India can supply green hydrogen and derivatives, such as green ammonia and green methanol, to countries seeking low-emission fuels. India’s renewable energy resources can support this supply. Exports can open industrial opportunities and strengthen India’s position in low-emission fuels.

India’s Green Hydrogen Production Potential
Bringing Cohesion in Government Approach
The Government has adopted an integrated strategy to increase the adoption of Green hydrogen across the sector. It coordinates with Central and State Ministries, Departments, agencies and institutions to drive adoption. Each Ministry has a defined role. For example,
Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas
promotes use in refineries and city gas distribution;
Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilisers
encourage indigenous green ammonia-based fertilisers;
Ministry of Road Transport and Highways
enable transport use through regulations, standards and codes;
Ministry of Steel
drives adoption in steelmaking;
Ministry of External Affairs
facilitates collaboration with global partners.
India’s Green Hydrogen Policy Architecture
NGHM: A mission for the whole ecosystem
MNRE is implementing the NGHM to make India a global hub for green hydrogen and its derivatives. The Union Cabinet approved the Mission in January 2023 with an outlay of Rs19,744 crore. It targets production capacity of at least 5 million metric tonnes (MMT) annually by 2030. With export demand, this could reach 10 MMT per year. The Mission has the following components.
SIGHT: Support on both sides of the market
The
Strategic Interventions for Green Hydrogen Transition (SIGHT)
Programme is a key NGHM component. Its outlay is Rs17,490 crore up to 2029–30. It offers incentives for two purposes: domestic electrolyser manufacturing and green hydrogen production. Together, they strengthen indigenous capability and speed up production.
Key Progress
Incentives have been awarded to 15 companies for 3,000 MW per annum of electrolyser manufacturing capacity. This reduces dependence on imported supply chains.
About 8,000 tonnes per annum of green hydrogen capacity had been commissioned by February 2026.
Incentives have been awarded for 8,62,000 tonnes per annum of green hydrogen production capacity.
Pilot Projects
The NGHM supports pilots that replace fossil fuels and feedstocks in hard-to-abate sectors. These include steel, heavy-duty mobility and shipping. The pilots aim to identify technological, regulatory and infrastructure gaps. They will also test supply chains and technology integration. Their findings will guide commercial-scale deployment and the policy support needed. The Mission has earmarked Rs455 crore for low-carbon steel up to 2029–30. It has also earmarked Rs496 crore for mobility and Rs115 crore for shipping up to 2025–26.
Key Progress
Five pilot projects have been sanctioned in the steel sector. Rs84 crore is sanctioned for testing 100% hydrogen injection.
Twelve projects will deploy 70 hydrogen vehicles: 27 buses and 43 trucks. These include fuel cell electric vehicles (FCEVs) and hydrogen internal combustion engine (H₂-ICE) vehicles.
The projects also cover 16 hydrogen refuelling stations across 21 routes. Financial assistance of Rs41.58 crore has been released.
V.O. Chidambaranar Port Authority has awarded a pilot project to develop bunkering and refuelling facilities for green methanol. The project costs Rs 38.12 crore, including an MNRE grant of Rs 35 crore.
Green Hydrogen Hubs and
Hydrogen Valley Innovation Clusters (HVIC)
Hydrogen is difficult to transport. To address this, the Mission promotes hubs and HVICs. This cluster approach brings production, consumption and infrastructure together. It improves project viability and enables economies of scale. Projects in designated hubs can also access Central and State scheme benefits. The Mission has an outlay of Rs 400 crore up to 2025–26 for hubs and related projects. These initiatives aim to attract green investment and accelerate innovation.
Key Progress
MNRE has recognised Deendayal Port (Kandla, Gujarat), V.O. Chidambaranar Port (Tuticorin, Tamil Nadu) and Paradip Port (Odisha) as hubs.
An indigenously built 1 MW green hydrogen plant was commissioned at Kandla Port in July 2025.
Four HVICs have been awarded: Jodhpur, Odisha, Pune and Kerala.
Enabling Policy Framework
The Mission follows a whole-of-government approach to make green hydrogen affordable. MNRE coordinates with Central and State departments on benefits and project facilitation. Key measures include waiving interstate transmission charges and facilitating renewable energy banking. They also include time-bound Open Access and grid connectivity. The Government will coordinate planning for renewable capacity, transmission, banking and storage. Solar Parks, Manufacturing Zones and Special Economic Zones (SEZs) may be extended to hydrogen facilities. The Mission will also explore international green finance, green bonds and innovative financing.
Key Progress
Green hydrogen and green ammonia plants commissioned by 31 December 2030 are
exempt from Inter-State Transmission System (ISTS)
charges for 25 years. ISTS are fees for moving power across state boundaries. The waiver lowers electricity costs.
The
Green Energy Corridor Scheme
supports lines and substations that carry renewable power to the grid. A national transmission plan improves links between generation and consumption centres.
Click to Read More
Duty benefits
under Section 26 of the Special Economic Zones Act, 2005, have been extended to eligible units installing and operating renewable energy equipment exclusively for captive consumption. This can reduce the cost of setting up renewable energy facilities within SEZs to meet their own electricity requirements.
Standalone plants producing green hydrogen or green ammonia through water electrolysis using renewable energy have been
exempted from prior Environmental Clearance
under the Environment Impact Assessment Notification, 2006. This can simplify the approval process for eligible projects.
Renewable energy plants located within a Special Economic Zone (SEZ) or Export Oriented Unit (EOU) are
exempt from the Approved List of Models and Manufacturers (ALMM) and Revised List of Models and Manufacturers (RLMM) requirements
when supplying electricity exclusively to green hydrogen production plants or their derivatives. This provides eligible projects greater flexibility in sourcing renewable energy equipment, subject to the applicable exemption conditions.
The Green Hydrogen and Green Ammonia Policy provides for
Open Access within 15 days
and
banking of surplus renewable electricity for up to 30 days
, subject to applicable provisions. Open Access allows producers to procure renewable electricity from sources other than their local distribution company. Banking allows surplus electricity to be stored as a credit and used later, subject to applicable regulations.
Regulations and Standards
The Mission is building regulations and standards aligned with industry needs. The aim is to enable sector growth and harmonise with international norms.
Key Progress
India’s Green Hydrogen Standard has been notified. It sets a ceiling of 2 kg CO₂ equivalent per kg of hydrogen, well-to-gate, averaged over a 12-month period. This created a common benchmark.
Scheme guidelines have been issued to fund testing facilities, infrastructure and institutional support for standards.
Standards for green ammonia and green methanol have been notified. They set emission thresholds and eligibility conditions, supporting production and trade.
MNRE launched the
Green Hydrogen Certification Scheme
of India in April 2025. The Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE) accredits agencies for monitoring, verification and certification.
A dedicated portal went live in June 2026 for transparent certification and compliance. Credible certification will help Indian producers compete with confidence globally.
Research and Development
The Mission supports research and development (R&D) to make green hydrogen more affordable, efficient, safe and reliable. The Strategic Hydrogen Innovation Partnership (SHIP) is a public-private framework, with a dedicated R&D fund from industry and Government. Scheme guidelines for R&D were notified in March 2024, with an outlay of Rs 400 crore. As of June 2026, an initial R&D roadmap worth Rs 113 crore is supporting approved projects across hydrogen production, storage, and safety technologies.
Skilling
A coordinated skill development initiative is under way. The Mission aims to generate over 6 lakh jobs across the value chain by 2030. So far, 8,149 candidates have been trained and 7,248 certified in hydrogen-related qualifications across 14 States and Union Territories. Training spans renewable power for electrolysers, electrolysis, storage, transport, safety standards and end use such as steel, mobility and refining. For innovation, Rs 100 crore has been allocated to start-ups working on green hydrogen technologies. The first nine start-ups have been approved, with total funding of Rs22 crore.
International Cooperation
The Mission promotes partnerships to develop technology, mobilise investment, build export markets and align standards.
Key Progress
MNRE, directly or through the National Institute of Solar Energy, has signed MoUs, Letters of Intent or Joint Declarations of Intent. The partners are Australia, Finland, France, Germany, Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Uzbekistan.
An MoU on renewable energy has been signed with the Netherlands.
An India–US Hydrogen Task Force has been formed under the Strategic Clean Energy Partnership.
Green hydrogen is a focus area of the India–US New and Emerging Renewable Energy Technology Action Platform (RETAP).
State-level Initiatives
Six States have notified dedicated green hydrogen policies, complementing the National Green Hydrogen Mission.
Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan and West Bengal
are the States with notified dedicated policies.
Four more States are finalising their dedicated green hydrogen policies. Haryana, Punjab, Bihar and Keralam are working on the draft policies.
Seven States have integrated hydrogen into their existing industrial and renewable energy policy frameworks. These include Himachal Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Odisha, Telangana and Chhattisgarh.
The Road Ahead
The National Green Hydrogen Mission marks an important step towards building a cleaner, more self-reliant and globally competitive energy economy. By 2030, India aims to develop
5 million metric tonnes (MMT) of annual green hydrogen production capacity
. This transition can reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels and strengthen the country’s long-term energy security. The Mission is expected to reduce cumulative fossil fuel imports by approximately
Rs1 lakh crore by 2030
.
Beyond energy security, the Mission seeks to create new opportunities for industrial growth, investment and employment. It is expected to mobilise over
Rs8 lakh crore in investments
and generate more than
6 lakh jobs
across manufacturing, infrastructure, research and project development. The production and use of the targeted green hydrogen quantum could also help avert nearly
50 MMT of carbon dioxide emissions annually
. Through these efforts, the Government aims to accelerate industrial decarbonisation, strengthen domestic manufacturing and position India as a global hub for green hydrogen production, use and exports. This will contribute to India’s broader vision of
Viksit Bharat by 2047
and its commitment to achieving
net-zero emissions by 2070
.

title: The NHRC, India issues an Advisory on the ‘Protection of Human Rights of Female Inmates and their Children’
subtitle:
The Advisory emphasises focused attention and a sensitive, gender-responsive approach to the rights and needs of women prisoners and their children

The ten key areas in the Advisory focus on action by the nine Union Ministries, Chief Secretaries/ Administrators, DGPs of all States and UTs

Urging action on its recommendations in the Advisory, the NHRC seeks reports from the concerned authorities within two months on the progress of their implementation
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                28 OCT 2026 12:11PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC), India has issued an Advisory on the ‘Protection of Human Rights of Female Inmates and their Children’ to nine Union Ministries, Chief Secretaries/ Administrators, Director Generals of Police of all States and Union Territories (UTs).
The NHRC emphasises that the rights and needs of prisoners, including the female prisoners and their children, who constitute a more vulnerable group among them, require focused attention and a sensitive, gender-responsive approach. Beyond custodial safeguards, it calls for humane prison conditions, adequate maternal and child healthcare, access to justice, preservation of family ties, protection of children's best interests, meaningful opportunities for rehabilitation and social reintegration.
The Advisory focuses on ten broad areas for action. These include Pre-Admission, Arrest and Entry into the Prison System, Admission Records, Child Database and Documentation, Health, Medical Care and Mental Health Services, Women Inmates: Living Conditions, Hygiene, Welfare and Sensitisation, Children Living with or Separated from Prisoners, Communication, Mulakat and Family Contact, Prison Administration, Legal Aid and Access to Justice, Gender-Responsive Facilities and Welfare Measures during Court Production of Women Inmates, Rehabilitation, Post-Release and Social Reintegration and Foreign National Inmates.
The detailed Advisory may be accessed at
https://nhrc.nic.in/flipbook/other_advisories/46
The NHRC urges all authorities concerned to implement the recommendations in the Advisory and furnish an Action Taken Report (ATR) within two months to keep it informed of the progress made.

title: Special Campaign 6.0: Department of Pharmaceuticals Focuses on E-Waste Management, Cleanliness, and Efficient Space Utilization; 14,700 cleanliness drives conducted, 2,200 sq. ft. of office space  freed up, ₹2.30 lakh earned from office scrap disposal
ministry: Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers :Department of Pharmaceuticals
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                28 OCT 2026 8:47PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Department of Pharmaceuticals (DoP), Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers, is actively participating in the
Special Campaign for Disposal of Pending Matters (SCDPM) 6.0
, along with its attached office, the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA), and its organisations, including the seven National Institutes of Pharmaceutical Education and Research (NIPERs), the Pharmaceuticals & Medical Devices Bureau of India (PMBI), and three Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs), namely Bengal Chemicals & Pharmaceuticals Limited (BCPL), Hindustan Antibiotics Limited (HAL), and Karnataka Antibiotics & Pharmaceuticals Limited (KAPL).
Being conducted from
October 2 to October 31, 2026
, the campaign focuses on promoting cleanliness, scientific management and disposal of e-waste, systematic record management, effective grievance redressal, and optimum utilisation of office space, with the objective of enhancing administrative efficiency and promoting a clean, organised, and productive work environment.
Field Office Outreach and Sustainable Workplace Practices:
Promoting Swachhata and environmental awareness forms a core pillar of the campaign. Across field and outstation offices,
14,700 cleanliness drives have been conducted so far against a baseline target of 12,208
, reflecting the Department’s continued efforts to improve workplace hygiene and sanitation, strengthen environmental awareness, and foster sustainable workplace practices.
Record Management and Optimum Utilisation of Office Space
The campaign has strengthened systematic record management and promoted the efficient utilisation of office space.
Against a baseline target of 2,716 physical files and 20 e-files
, the Department has reviewed
4,283 physical files and 20 e-files
, while
489 files have been weeded out and closed
. Additionally,
2,200 square feet of office space has been freed up
through these efforts, contributing to better space management and the creation of more organised, efficient, and clutter-free workplaces.
Grievance Redressal and Liquidation of Pendency
Administrative efficiency and responsive governance are being strengthened through the timely resolution of pending matters, including
MP references (3 against target of 4), parliamentary assurances(1 out of 2), a Cabinet proposal (02 proposals), State reference (57 against 58) and PMO references (02 cases)
.
Against the target of 72 public grievances and 28 appeals, registered on the Centralised Public Grievance Redress and Monitoring System (CPGRAMS), 132 public grievance cases and 39 appeals have been settled. Against target of 20 items identified for easing of rules/processes, this has been completed for 17 items
. These efforts aim to expedite the resolution of pending matters, improve service delivery, and promote greater accountability and efficiency in public administration.
Scientific E-Waste Management and Responsible Disposal
Scientific e-waste management is one of the key focus areas of
SCDPM 6
. The Department has targeted
1,011 obsolete electronic and electrical items
- comprising IT equipment, consumer electronics, appliances, and laboratory tools - for safe disposal through empanelled recyclers under the E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022. The process for disposing of these items is currently underway.
Further, the Department has earned a revenue of ₹2,30,187/- from the disposal of office scrap. Department of Pharmaceuticals remains committed to the objectives of SCDPM 6 and is monitoring targets closely and documenting achievements via the National Special Campaign Portal.
